note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Interpret an assessment question's steer and keywords before writing

evidence.title: Question analysis sheet read through the academic literacies lens
evidence.example: You take one essay question and mark up its steer (the instruction word) and its keywords, then write two sentences on what each asks you to do. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note that knowing what a tutor means by a steer is part of academic socialisation into a subject, not a fixed rule (for example, what "assess" asks for in a geography question on flood management). This shows you can interpret a question before you start writing.
evidence.artefact: A marked-up assessment question with the steer and keywords labelled and a short note on what each asks for.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998

evidence.title: Annotated brief for your first marked assignment
evidence.example: Before starting your first marked assignment, you annotate the brief: the steer, the keywords, the word count and the marking criteria. You then check your reading with your tutor or at a writing support drop-in (for example, a first-year nursing reflection that asks you to "discuss" a care episode, not describe it). This shows you read a brief to find out what is being asked before you begin.
evidence.artefact: The annotated assignment brief with a dated note of the tutor's or adviser's confirmation of your reading.
grounding: professional: Reads a brief to establish what is being asked, by whom and against what criteria before starting work.

capabilities.statement: Follow the writing cycle to plan and complete a first draft

evidence.title: Writing process log mapped to the writing cycle
evidence.example: You keep a short log while you write one essay, recording what you did at each stage of the writing cycle and labelling it with Flower and Hayes' (1981) planning, translating and reviewing. Using Lea and Street (1998), you add a note on which conventions you were still learning (for example, how to open a 1,000-word sociology essay). This shows you followed a set method from plan to a complete first draft.
evidence.artefact: A one-page process log with dated entries for each stage of the writing cycle, attached to your plan and first draft.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998
model: Cognitive process theory of writing (Flower and Hayes 1981)

evidence.title: Society end-of-year report planned and drafted
evidence.example: As a committee member of a student society, you are asked to write the end-of-year report for the students' union. You make a plan of headings first, write a full rough draft in one sitting, and only then tidy it (for example, a film society report covering screenings, membership and spending). This shows you can plan a document and get a complete first draft down before polishing.
evidence.artefact: Your dated plan, the unpolished first draft and the final submitted report, kept together as one portfolio page.
grounding: professional: Plans a document and gets a full working draft down before polishing it.

capabilities.statement: Find and correct errors in own writing by proofreading and editing

evidence.title: Two-pass error log separating editing from proofreading
evidence.example: You review one of your drafts in two separate passes: an editing pass for meaning and order, then a proofreading pass for surface errors such as comma splices. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note that error-spotting alone matches their study skills model, and that editing also asks what your subject expects (for example, a psychology lab report). This shows you can find and correct errors in your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A marked-up draft with an error log sorting each correction into editing or proofreading, with the type of error named.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998

evidence.title: Proofread volunteer handbook update for a food bank
evidence.example: Volunteering at a local food bank, you are asked to check an updated volunteer handbook before it is printed. You read it once for sense and once for errors, keep to the organisation's style, and send back a list of corrections (for example, inconsistent opening times and a run-on sentence in the safety section). This shows you can check and correct a document before it goes out.
evidence.artefact: The tracked-changes copy of the handbook and a short email from the coordinator confirming the corrections were used.
grounding: professional: Checks and corrects documents before they go out.

capabilities.statement: Identify and structure the essay and other argued genres

evidence.title: Genre map comparing an essay and a problem question
evidence.example: You compare two argued genres in your subject and map how each is structured, using Swales' (1990) idea that a genre belongs to a discourse community with shared purposes. With Lea and Street (1998), you explain why tutors expect each structure (for example, a law essay that argues a position versus a problem question that applies the law to facts). You then choose and justify the structure for your own assignment.
evidence.artefact: A side-by-side structural map of two genres, annotated, with a paragraph justifying the structure used in your own assignment.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998
model: Genre analysis and discourse community (Swales 1990)

evidence.title: Choosing the right document type on a placement
evidence.example: On a placement in a software team, you are asked to make the case for changing a testing process. You decide whether a briefing note, report or proposal suits the reader, explain your choice and structure the document to fit it (for example, a two-page proposal for a team lead with a costed option). This shows you can identify an argued genre and structure it for its purpose.
evidence.artefact: The finished document with a short written rationale for the genre chosen and your supervisor's feedback on it.
grounding: professional: Chooses and follows the right document type (briefing, report, case note, proposal) for the reader and purpose.

capabilities.statement: Write clear sentences in the active voice

evidence.title: Sentence rewrite commentary on active and passive voice
evidence.example: You take a paragraph of your own and rewrite it in subject, verb, object order, changing passive sentences to active ones where that makes them clearer. Using Lea and Street (1998), you judge where the passive is a disciplinary convention and where it only hides who did what (for example, a chemistry method versus the discussion section). This shows you construct clear sentences and choose voice deliberately.
evidence.artefact: A before-and-after paragraph with a commentary explaining each change and each passive sentence you chose to keep.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998

evidence.title: Plain English customer email template at work
evidence.example: In a part-time job in a customer contact centre, you rewrite a standard email that customers often misread. You shorten sentences, put the person doing the action first and cut jargon, then ask colleagues to test it (for example, a refund email that now says "We will refund you within five days"). This shows you write plain, active English a busy reader understands first time.
evidence.artefact: The old and new email templates side by side with notes on each change and your manager's approval.
grounding: professional: Writes in plain, active English that a busy reader understands first time.

capabilities.statement: Use the four pillars to review and structure own writing

evidence.title: Reverse outline review using the four pillars
evidence.example: You use the guide's four pillars of effective writing as a self-review lens on a full essay draft. You reverse outline it, checking that each paragraph has a topic sentence and one point, and restructure where it does not. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note which choices follow your subject's expectations (for example, an education essay on inclusive classroom practice). This shows you evaluate and restructure your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A reverse outline of your draft before and after revision, with notes against each pillar on what you changed.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998

evidence.title: Restructured report for a museum live brief
evidence.example: On a live brief for a local museum, you write a report on visitor feedback. You plan it so each section and paragraph makes one point, then move the recommendations to the front because the client reads those first (for example, a history module project on a new gallery trail). You explain how this differs from an essay that builds to its conclusion. This shows you can organise writing so a reader can follow it.
evidence.artefact: The client report with a short note on its structure and the museum contact's written response to it.
grounding: professional: Organises a document so that each section and paragraph makes one point the reader can follow.

capabilities.statement: Recognise how writing conventions vary by discipline

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of writing conventions across three disciplines
evidence.example: You collect three published extracts from different disciplines and analyse their conventions: voice, use of evidence, structure and hedging. Using Lea and Street's (1998) academic literacies model, you argue that these differences reflect each discipline's ways of making knowledge, not right or wrong styles (for example, as a joint honours biology and philosophy student comparing a results section with an argued paper). You then apply your findings to your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A comparative table of conventions across three annotated extracts, with a commentary on how you adapted your own writing.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998
model: Genre analysis and discourse community (Swales 1990)

evidence.title: Technical and public versions of the same findings
evidence.example: On a placement with an environmental consultancy, you write up a habitat survey in the firm's technical format, then adapt it for a community consultation. You decide what to keep, what to explain and what to drop for each audience (for example, turning species tables into a plain summary of what the development means locally). This shows you write in a profession's conventions and adapt them for readers outside it.
evidence.artefact: The paired technical and public documents with a reflective note on the conventions you changed, signed by your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Writes in the conventions of one's profession and adapts them for readers outside it.

capabilities.statement: Integrate sources actively, own point first

evidence.title: Voice audit of literature review paragraphs
evidence.example: You audit three paragraphs of your literature review, highlighting your own claims and the sources in different colours. Drawing on Lea and Street's (1998) attention to authority and identity in student writing, you rewrite paragraphs led by sources so each opens with your point, uses paraphrase, and uses sources to support or qualify it (for example, a criminology review on desistance). This shows you integrate sources actively with your own point first.
evidence.artefact: Colour-coded before-and-after paragraphs with a commentary on how your voice and the sources' voices now relate.
grounding: ing:doc:academic-literacies-lea-street-1998

evidence.title: Evidence-led recommendation paper for a sports club
evidence.example: Working with a university sports club, you write a short paper recommending a change to how coaches monitor training load. You lead with your recommendation, then cite the research and the club's own data that support or qualify it (for example, injury records set against two sport science studies). This shows you can put your own point first and use evidence to back it in a real setting.
evidence.artefact: The recommendation paper with its reference list and the head coach's written response, showing whether the change was adopted.
grounding: professional: Leads with one's own recommendation and cites the evidence that supports or qualifies it.

evidence.title: Writer's positioning statement for a master's dissertation
evidence.example: You write a reflective statement on how you position yourself as an author in your dissertation, using Ivanic's (1998) distinction between the autobiographical self, the discoursal self and the self as author, and Lea and Street's (1998) academic literacies model (for example, a public health dissertation where you write as a former practitioner). You show how your choices of voice and evidence fit, or knowingly depart from, your discipline's conventions.
evidence.artefact: A 1,000-word positioning statement with excerpts from your dissertation annotated to show deliberate authorial choices.
grounding: model: Writer identity (Ivanic 1998)
model: Academic literacies (Lea and Street 1998)

evidence.title: Writing portfolio for specialist and non-specialist readers
evidence.example: On an industry-sponsored engineering project, you write for three readers: a technical report for the sponsor, a lay summary for site staff and a short conference abstract. You then reflect on how your writing moved between these communities and what each demanded of you (for example, how much uncertainty to state for each reader). This shows you write with awareness of your discipline and its wider context.
evidence.artefact: A portfolio of the three pieces with a reflective commentary on your disciplinary writing choices and the sponsor's feedback.
grounding: practice: industry-sponsored postgraduate project
